title: Indocyanine Green Fluorescence Angiography in Colorectal Cancer Surgery After a Decade of Randomized Trials: From Visual Assessment to Quantification and Beyond
content: Anastomotic leakage (AL) remains one of the most serious complications of colorectal cancer surgery, and inadequate perfusion is one of the few causes that surgeons can cor-rect intraoperatively. Indocyanine green fluorescence angiography (ICG-FA) shows intes-tinal perfusion in real time and is widely used. Meta-analyses of randomized trials show that ICG-FA reduces overall AL by about one-third, mainly after left-sided and rectal anastomoses, although most individual trials missed their primary endpoints, and effects after right-sided resection and on grade C AL remain unproven. We explore why the trials appeared to disagree and what this implies for perfusion assessment. We consider statis-tical precision, anatomical site, leak severity, endpoints, diversion and neoadjuvant treat-ment, imaging protocols, and interpretation, then review quantitative perfusion analysis, hyperspectral and laser speckle contrast imaging, near-infrared-II imaging, and artificial intelligence. The apparent disagreement is compatible with limited precision for a moder-ate common effect, as the trials were powered for reductions of about 40% or more; differ-ences in endpoints and technique mean that they answered somewhat different questions. Separately, imaging physics and observer variability suggest that the weak point of ICG-FA is how fluorescence is measured and read. Until objective methods are shown to improve clinical outcomes, ICG-FA should be performed with a standardized protocol.
